schemaNotes: Every rate is a fraction, the same unit as the report's assumptions.taxRate (6.25% is 0.0625). combinedLow/combinedHigh is the state rate plus the lowest and highest local add-on found for vehicle sales, as a single fraction each, not a local-only add-on. A null field always means unknown: a confirmed 'none' or 'not applicable' goes in note instead, so null keeps one meaning. This covers a deliberate handful of states for range of coverage, not population. See locale.md for what to do with a state not listed here, and calc.py state --code XX to read one row without loading the whole file.

TX.name: Texas
TX.privatePartyRule: Tax is on the greater of the sales price (total consideration) or 80% of the vehicle's standard presumptive value (SPV), unless the buyer presents a certified appraisal (Comptroller Form 14-128) within 30 days (60 for active-duty military) showing a lower value.

source.title: Texas Comptroller, Motor Vehicle Tax Guide 96-254: Total Consideration

TX.note: The 6.25% rate is flat statewide, with no local add-on for the motor vehicle sales tax itself (unlike Texas's general sales tax, which does have local add-ons). A separately stated documentary fee has been excluded from the taxable total consideration since 1971, per Comptroller guidance, so docFeeTaxed is false. Separately stated manufacturer rebates are excluded too. A trade-in's value does reduce the taxable amount on a dealer sale. A dealer's special inventory tax is a property tax the dealer owes the county on past sales. It's not a line item on the buyer's invoice, so it doesn't belong in the buyer's OTD price.

CA.name: California
specialLineItems: California tire fee: $1.75 per new tire, stated separately, not itself subject to sales tax

source.title: CDTFA, California City & County Sales & Use Tax Rates

CA.note: No trade-in credit: tax applies to the full price, including the dealer's trade-in allowance, per CDTFA's own annotations (Rev. and Tax. Code 6012(b)(2), Regulation 1654(b)(1), at cdtfa.ca.gov/lawguides/vol2/suta/140-0500.html). CDTFA's own page (effective Oct 1, 2026) confirms a 7.25% statewide base plus district add-ons of 0.10% to 2.00%, a 9.25% arithmetic ceiling, but it also says some addresses stack more than one district. combinedHigh here (0.1125) is the combined rate in a stacked-district city. Look up the exact rate for the buyer's registration address on CDTFA's own county-and-city table. The $85 doc fee cap (Vehicle Code 4456.5) may be lower for dealers outside the DMV's private-industry partner program, so verify which applies. The yearly figure is a state fee (the vehicle license fee, about 0.65% of value, paid at registration each year), not a county property tax.

GA.name: Georgia
GA.privatePartyRule: The Title Ad Valorem Tax (TAVT) is 7% of the state's own fair market value for the model, from the Department of Revenue's assessment manual (or a designated used-car market guide), regardless of the price actually paid. A trade-in reduces the taxable base only on a dealer sale, not a private-party sale.

source.title: Georgia Department of Revenue, Title Ad Valorem Tax (TAVT) FAQ

GA.note: TAVT replaces the sales tax on the vehicle. It's a one-time title tax paid once at titling, not layered on top of a separate sales tax. A reduced 3% rate applies to a vehicle already titled elsewhere by a new Georgia resident, and 0.5% to a family transfer where TAVT was already paid.

NC.name: North Carolina
NC.privatePartyRule: A private-party sale is taxed on NCDMV's own assessed "computer value" for the vehicle, not the price actually paid.

source.title: NCDMV, Vehicle Titles and Registration Taxes and Fees

NC.note: The 3% highway use tax is a one-time tax at titling, in place of a sales tax, applied to price plus any doc fee minus a dealer trade-in. Separately, North Carolina bills an annual vehicle property tax with registration renewal ("Tag & Tax Together"). That rate is the local county/city property-tax rate, so there's no single statewide figure to give here: roughRate is null rather than a guess. Dealer doc fees typically run about $500 to $800.

OR.name: Oregon
OR.privatePartyRule: No sales tax applies to a private-party sale.

source.title: Oregon Department of Revenue, Vehicle Privilege and Use Taxes

OR.note: Oregon has no state or local sales tax. A dealer selling a vehicle that's never been titled in Oregon owes a separate 0.5% vehicle privilege tax and may itemize and pass that amount to the buyer. It's a tax on the dealer, collected through the buyer, so it's left out of taxRate here.

VA.name: Virginia

source.title: Virginia DMV, Sales and Use Tax (SUT)

VA.note: The Code of Virginia (58.1-2402) carries two contingent versions of this rate (4.15% and 3%), tied to a 2019 transportation-funding trigger. The DMV's own current page states 4.15%, with a $75 minimum tax, so that's the figure used here. By statute (58.1-2405), no trade-in credit reduces this tax, unlike most states. The yearly figure is a local personal property tax, billed by the city or county where the car is garaged, not a state tax. Rates run roughly 1.6% to 5% of assessed value depending on locality (examples: Prince William County $3.50/$100 for 2026, Loudoun County $3.09/$100 for 2026), often with a relief percentage on the first $20,000 of value. 0.035 here is a rough statewide midpoint, not any specific locality's rate.

NY.name: New York

source.title: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, Publication 838 (A Guide to Sales Tax for Automobile Dealers)

NY.note: Tax is based on the combined rate where the buyer lives, not where the dealer is, so look up the buyer's own locality. The high end (8.875%) is New York City's combined rate. Other localities run lower. The $175 doc fee cap comes from regulation 15 NYCRR 78.19.
